extracted.intended_audience: NLP / machine learning researchers and practitioners working on humor detection
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation and comparison of machine learning and deep learning techniques for classifying short social-media texts (tweets) as humorous or non-humorous using a Kaggle corpus; includes dataset preparation, feature representations, model selection, and performance measurement. Suitable for experimental NLP studies of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall classification accuracy for humor prediction (the paper states enhanced accuracy was obtained for humor prediction using deep learning as compared to machine learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a primary comparative metric to report model performance; the paper emphasizes accuracy improvements when using deep learning (CNN, LSTM) versus traditional ML classifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision, recall and F-score
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of precision, recall and f-score as discriminant measures for performance evaluation (cites Sokolova et al. and Goutte & Gaussier for probabilistic interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate class-wise performance and harmonic-mean tradeoffs (F-score) rather than relying solely on accuracy; referenced literature for interpretation and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) / other discriminant measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ROC and a broader family of discriminant measures beyond accuracy and F-score for performance evaluation (reference: 'Beyond accuracy, f-score and ROC: a family of discriminant measures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ROC analysis where appropriate to assess classifier discrimination capability across thresholds; consider alternatives from cited work for more nuanced assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion-matrix-based feature selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature selection and evaluation techniques that leverage the confusion matrix (reference: 'Confusion matrix-based feature selection').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confusion-matrix-derived statistics to inform feature selection and understand types of classification errors; can guide feature engineering and model tuning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train/test dataset split and dataset provenance (Kaggle CSV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a Kaggle dataset containing humorous and non-humorous tweets provided in separate train and test CSV files; explicit train/test separation for experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure datasets are clearly partitioned into train and test sets; visualize and inspect the train dataset (paper links a Kaggle train-dataset visualization). Report dataset source and formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model selection and comparative algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare multiple machine learning and deep learning algorithms: logistic regression, decision tree, random forests, passive aggressive classifier (ML) and CNN, LSTM (deep learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform comparative analysis across representative ML and DL models to determine relative performance; report hyperparameters, training regimen, and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word representations / embeddings (GloVe, BERT/ColBERT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of dense word/sentence representations such as GloVe and BERT-based embeddings (ColBERT) for capturing semantic features useful in humor detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pre-trained embeddings or contextual sentence embeddings to improve feature representation; citations provided (Pennington et al. for GloVe, Annamoradnejad & Zoghi for ColBERT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of humor's subjective, cognitive and cultural factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that humor is subjective and multifactorial — cognitive and cultural knowledge affect what is humorous and thus should be considered when modeling and evaluating humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design datasets, features, and evaluation protocols that account for cultural and cognitive variability (e.g., annotate or stratify by demographic/cultural variables, use diverse examples). Acknowledge limits on generalization due to subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task decomposition: punchline detection, double entendre and wordplay recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtasks relevant to automatic humor understanding include punchline detection, double entendre identification, and computational recognition of wordplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider treating humor detection as composed of specialized subtasks (e.g., punchline localization, figurative language detection) and evaluate subsystem performance; citations include Kiddon & Brun (double entendre) and Taylor & Mazlack (wordplay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative example generation and dataset augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generation of negative examples (non-humorous instances) as part of dataset construction or augmentation to improve distinction between humorous and non-humorous text (reference: Winters & Delobelle 'Generating Negative Examples').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use methods to synthesize or select challenging negative examples to make classifiers more robust; report how negatives were generated and analyze their effect on performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction of funniness score (regression/scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond binary humor detection, prediction of a funniness score (degree of humor) is a related evaluation target (reference: TECHSSN at HAHA 2021: 'humor detection and funniness score prediction').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If modeling funniness intensity, adopt appropriate regression or ordinal evaluation metrics and report corresponding error/fit measures; cite relevant shared-task approaches.
